problem: The sentence says a compiler or interpreter turns source into machine instructions 'often called binaries'. An interpreter does not produce machine instructions or a binary file; it executes the source statements directly. A student can take away the wrong model.
fix: A compiler translates the source into machine instructions and usually writes a binary file; an interpreter reads the source and executes it directly, without producing a separate binary.

problem: The sentence attributes the no-per-user cost to the licence, but an open-source licence never charges a fee; any per-seat charge comes from a vendor's support or subscription plan. As written it sounds as if some open-source licences do charge per seat.
fix: The licence itself charges nothing and has no per-seat condition, so the legal cost does not grow with every extra user or lab PC. A vendor may still sell per-seat support contracts.

problem: The comparison sets the open-source total (licence plus support) against the proprietary licence alone, so the saving looks larger than it would be in a fair comparison. The section itself warns to compare like with like, and a student may copy this method in the exam.
fix: Keep the arithmetic but add one line: the proprietary route also has support, training and migration costs, so the true saving is smaller; the figure shown is only against the licence line, as the question states.

problem: 'Linux runs ... Android phones' can read as if Android were a Linux distribution like the ones in this course. Android uses the Linux kernel but is not a normal Linux system.
fix: Linux runs most web servers and many government systems, and the Android kernel is Linux.

problem: 'Long-term use improves because the source survives' is vague — what improves is continuity and the ability to keep maintaining the software, not the software by itself.
fix: Long-term continuity improves because the source survives even if the original vendor stops selling or supporting the product, so another team can keep it running.
